chapters.n: The title calls this “the song of songs” — the greatest or most beautiful song. It is a collection of love poetry between a bride and her bridegroom, connected with Solomon. In his Bible revision, Joseph Smith noted that he did not regard this book as inspired scripture.

f.g: A Hebrew superlative, like “holy of holies” — the finest song.
JST manuscript note: “The Songs of Solomon are not inspired writings.”

chapters.n: The bride speaks first, longing for her beloved’s affection. She says his love is more delightful than wine, the drink of celebration.

f.g: Wine symbolized joy and festivity in ancient Israel.

chapters.n: His fragrance is lovely, and his very name — his character and reputation — is like perfume poured out. No wonder the young women admire him.

f.g: Fragrance.
Young women; maidens.

chapters.n: She asks him to draw her close. She has been brought into the king’s rooms, and her friends join in rejoicing at their love.

f.g: Take me with you; pull me near.
Or “rightly do they love you.”

chapters.n: She tells the women of Jerusalem that though her skin is dark from the sun, she is lovely — like the black goat-hair tents of Kedar or the fine curtains of Solomon.

f.g: An Arabian desert tribe descended from Ishmael, known for black tents (Genesis 25:13).
Lovely, attractive.

chapters.n: She explains her sun-darkened skin: her angry brothers made her work outdoors in the vineyards, so she couldn’t care for her own “vineyard” — her own appearance.

f.g: Her brothers.
Probably herself — her beauty and person.

chapters.n: She asks her beloved, pictured as a shepherd, where he rests his flock at noon, so she doesn’t have to wander among other shepherds looking for him.

f.g: Or “one who is veiled” — wandering about like a stranger.

chapters.n: The answer (perhaps from him or from her friends): follow the tracks of the flock and graze your young goats near the shepherds’ tents, and you’ll find him.

f.g: Young goats.

chapters.n: Now the bridegroom speaks. He compares her to a splendid mare among Pharaoh’s chariot horses — a compliment to her beauty and grace that stood out.
Her face is beautiful framed by strings of jewelry, and her neck by golden necklaces.

f.g: Strings of beads or ornaments.

chapters.n: He (or the friends) promises to make her even finer ornaments of gold and silver.

f.g: Small ornaments or beads.

chapters.n: The bride says that while the king reclines at his table, her perfume spreads its fragrance — a way of saying her love reaches out to him.

f.g: Nard, a costly fragrant oil from the Himalayas (compare Mark 14:3).

chapters.n: She describes her beloved as a little pouch of myrrh worn close to her heart — precious and always near.

f.g: A fragrant resin often worn in a small bag around the neck.
Between.

chapters.n: He is to her like a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi, a lush oasis beside the Dead Sea.

f.g: Henna, a shrub with fragrant blossoms.
A spring-fed oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea (1 Samuel 24:1).

chapters.n: The groom praises her beauty twice for emphasis. Her eyes are like doves — gentle, soft, and faithful.

f.g: A picture of gentleness, innocence, and constancy.

chapters.n: She answers that he is handsome and delightful. Their resting place is like green grass, a picture of a fresh, peaceful setting.
Their “house” is like a forest of cedar and fir — whether a real garden setting or a poetic home, it is beautiful and strong.

f.g: Prized, fragrant wood from Lebanon, used in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:9).

chapters.n: The bride humbly calls herself a common wildflower of the Sharon plain and the valleys. Many Christians later applied the phrase “rose of Sharon” to Christ, though here the bride speaks of herself.

f.g: Probably a crocus or similar wildflower of the coastal plain of Sharon.

chapters.n: The groom answers: compared to other young women, she is like a lily surrounded by thorns.
She replies that compared to other young men, he is like a fruit tree in a forest — offering shade and sweet fruit.

f.g: Possibly the apricot or apple tree.
Shade was precious in a hot land — a picture of protection and rest.

chapters.n: He brought her to the banquet hall, and his love was displayed over her like a banner — openly and proudly.

f.g: Literally “house of wine.”
A flag or standard showing whom one belongs to.

chapters.n: She asks to be refreshed with raisin cakes and fruit, because she is faint with love.

f.g: Sustain or support me.
Better “raisin cakes.”

chapters.n: She describes his tender embrace and how secure she feels in his arms.
A refrain repeated in the book: she urges the young women not to awaken love before its proper time. Love should not be rushed.

f.g: Gazelles.
Female deer.

f.r: Song of Solomon 3:5; Song of Solomon 8:4

chapters.n: She hears his voice! He comes bounding over the mountains and hills, eager to see her.
He is like a swift gazelle or young stag. Now he stands outside her wall, peering through the window lattice.

f.g: A male deer.
A wooden screen over a window.

chapters.n: He calls her to get up and come away with him.
Winter is over and the rainy season has ended. In Israel, the rains fall from about October to April.
Flowers bloom, birds sing, and the cooing of the turtledove is heard. Spring is a picture of love coming to life.

f.g: Turtledove, a migrating bird that arrives in spring.

chapters.n: The first figs ripen and the blossoming vines give off fragrance. Again he invites her to come away with him.

f.g: The early, unripe figs that appear in spring.

chapters.n: He calls her his dove hidden in the rock clefts and cliff ledges, longing to see her face and hear her voice.

f.g: Steep cliffs or terraces.

chapters.n: Catch the little foxes that ruin the vineyards in bloom. Small problems, left alone, can damage a young and tender love.

f.g: Small pests that dig and gnaw at vines — a picture of small threats to love.

chapters.n: She declares their mutual commitment: he belongs to her and she to him. He pastures his flock among the lilies.

f.w: My beloved is mine, and I am his
f.r: Song of Solomon 6:3; Song of Solomon 7:10

chapters.n: She asks him to return quickly, like a gazelle on the rugged mountains, until morning breaks and the shadows flee.

f.g: Possibly “separation” or “cleft” — rugged, divided hills; the location is uncertain.

chapters.n: At night the bride searches for the one she loves but cannot find him. This may be a dream or a poetic picture of longing.

f.g: Repeated four times in verses 1–4 — her whole being longs for him.

chapters.n: She resolves to get up and search the city streets and squares for him, but still doesn’t find him.

f.g: Open squares or plazas.

chapters.n: The city watchmen find her, and she asks if they have seen her beloved.

f.g: Night guards who patrolled the city.

chapters.n: Soon after, she finds him and holds on tight, bringing him to her mother’s house — a sign of honorable, family-approved love.
The refrain returns: don’t awaken love until it is ready.

f.r: Song of Solomon 2:7; Song of Solomon 8:4

chapters.n: A new scene: a wedding procession appears from the wilderness, rising like columns of smoke from burning incense and fragrant spices.

f.g: Columns of incense smoke — or the dust raised by a great procession.
A costly fragrant resin.

chapters.n: Here comes Solomon’s royal carriage, guarded by sixty of Israel’s mightiest soldiers.

f.g: A litter or sedan chair carried by bearers.
Sixty (three times twenty).

chapters.n: Each guard is skilled in battle, sword at his side, ready to defend against any danger in the night.
Solomon built this carriage from the fine timber of Lebanon.

f.g: A palanquin — an elegant covered carriage.

chapters.n: Its posts were silver, its base gold, its seat purple, and its interior lovingly decorated by the women of Jerusalem.

f.g: An expensive dye used for royalty.
Lovingly inlaid or decorated.

chapters.n: The women of Zion are invited to come and see King Solomon wearing the crown his mother placed on him on his wedding day, the happiest day of his life.

f.g: Wedding.
Bathsheba (1 Kings 1:11-31).

chapters.n: The bridegroom begins a poem praising his bride’s beauty. Her eyes behind her veil are gentle as doves, and her flowing dark hair is like a flock of black goats streaming down the hills of Gilead.

f.g: Better “veil.”
Hill country east of the Jordan River, known for its pastures.

chapters.n: Her teeth are white and even, like freshly washed sheep, perfectly matched with none missing.

f.g: Freshly sheared.
Each tooth has its match — a complete, even set.

chapters.n: Her lips are like a scarlet ribbon, her speech lovely, and her cheeks behind her veil glow like the red of a sliced pomegranate.

f.g: Cheeks or brow.

chapters.n: Her neck is tall and dignified like David’s fortress tower, hung with shields. Her necklaces may be pictured as those shields.

f.g: Small round shields.

chapters.n: He describes her beauty with images of gentle twin gazelles grazing among lilies — soft, graceful, and lovely.

f.g: Gazelles.

chapters.n: He resolves to stay with her until morning, describing her as a fragrant hill of spices.
She is completely beautiful to him, without a single flaw. Paul uses similar language of Christ’s Church as His bride.

f.w: there is no spot in thee

chapters.n: He calls her to come with him from the high, wild mountains of the north — Lebanon, Amana, Senir, and Hermon — places of lions and leopards. He wants her safe by his side.

f.g: Senir, the Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9).
A peak in the Anti-Lebanon range.

chapters.n: She has captured his heart with a single glance. “Sister” was an affectionate term for a bride in ancient love poetry, not a family relationship.

f.g: Captivated; stolen away.
A term of tender closeness common in ancient Near Eastern love songs.

chapters.n: Her love is better than wine, and her fragrance sweeter than any spice. He echoes the praise she first gave him (1:2).

f.w: better is thy love than wine

chapters.n: Her words are sweet as honey and milk, and her clothing smells like the cedar forests of Lebanon. “Milk and honey” recalls the promised land.
She is like a private garden, a sealed spring — pure and reserved for her husband alone. The image honors faithfulness and chastity.

f.g: A walled garden, protected from outsiders.

chapters.n: Her “garden” is full of choice plants — pomegranates, henna, and nard. Every good thing is found in her.

f.g: Henna.

chapters.n: The list of rare spices continues — saffron, fragrant cane, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes. Many were costly imports, showing how precious she is.

f.g: A fragrant reed or cane, also used in holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).
Fragrant aloeswood, not the medicinal plant.

chapters.n: She is a fountain that waters gardens, a well of fresh, flowing water like mountain streams from Lebanon — a source of life.

f.g: Fresh, flowing water rather than still cistern water.

chapters.n: The bride answers, inviting the winds to spread the fragrance of her garden and welcoming her beloved into it — a poetic picture of giving herself to him in marriage.

f.g: She now calls the garden his — her love is freely given.

chapters.n: The groom responds that he has come into his garden and enjoyed its gifts. A voice — perhaps friends or the poet — then blesses the couple’s love.

f.g: Possibly wedding guests encouraging the couple, or the poet speaking.

chapters.n: The bride describes a dreamlike night: half-asleep, she hears her beloved knocking, asking to come in, his hair wet with night dew.

f.w: I sleep, but my heart waketh
f.g: Half-asleep or dreaming.
Perfect, flawless one.

chapters.n: She hesitates, making excuses: she’s already undressed and washed her feet for bed.

f.g: Tunic or robe.

chapters.n: He reaches through the door’s latch opening, and her heart stirs for him.

f.g: In Hebrew thought, the seat of deep feeling — “my heart was moved.”
An opening for reaching the latch.

chapters.n: She gets up to open the door, her hands dripping with perfumed myrrh on the lock.
But when she opens, he is gone. She is crushed, searches, and calls, but gets no answer. Delay can mean missed opportunities.

f.g: My heart sank.

chapters.n: The city watchmen find her, beat her, and take her cloak. Her search costs her dearly.

f.g: A shawl or outer cloak.

chapters.n: She asks the women of Jerusalem to tell her beloved, if they find him, that she is faint with love.
The women ask what makes her beloved so special that she pleads like this.
She answers that he is radiant and healthy, outstanding among ten thousand.

f.g: Radiant and with a healthy reddish complexion — compare David (1 Samuel 16:12).
Literally “bannered” — one who stands out like a flag above a crowd.

chapters.n: His head is like the finest gold, and his hair is wavy and black as a raven.

f.g: Wavy, curly.

chapters.n: His eyes are gentle like doves beside streams, bright and well placed.

f.g: Set like jewels in a setting.

chapters.n: His cheeks are fragrant like a bed of spices, and his lips are like lilies dripping with myrrh.
His arms are like rods of gold set with jewels, and his body like polished ivory decorated with sapphires. She describes him like a precious statue.

f.g: A precious stone, perhaps topaz or chrysolite.
Body or torso.

chapters.n: His legs are strong like marble pillars on golden bases, and his whole appearance is majestic like Lebanon’s cedars.

f.g: Bases or pedestals.

chapters.n: His words are sweet, and everything about him is desirable. He is not only her beloved but her friend — a beautiful ideal for marriage.

f.g: Literally “all of him is desirable.”
Friendship is part of true married love.

chapters.n: Moved by her description, the women ask where her beloved has gone so they can help her look.

f.g: Gone off to.

chapters.n: She knows where he is: in his garden among the spices and lilies. The garden again stands for their shared love.
She restates their bond: she belongs to him and he to her. The love is fully mutual.

f.w: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine
f.r: Song of Solomon 2:16; Song of Solomon 7:10

chapters.n: He praises her as beautiful as Tirzah and lovely as Jerusalem — two royal cities — and as awe-inspiring as an army with banners flying.

f.g: A beautiful city whose name means “pleasing”; later capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23).
Awe-inspiring, overwhelming.

chapters.n: Her eyes overwhelm him so much he asks her to look away. He repeats earlier praises of her hair.

f.g: Overwhelmed or unsettled me.

f.w: thy hair is as a flock of goats

chapters.n: He repeats his praise of her bright, even teeth.
Her cheeks behind her veil are like slices of pomegranate.
A king might have sixty queens, eighty concubines, and countless maidens.

f.g: Sixty.
Eighty.
Secondary wives in ancient royal households.

chapters.n: But his dove, his perfect one, is unique — her mother’s favorite. Even queens and the other women praise her. To him, she is the only one.

f.g: Unique, one of a kind.

chapters.n: Others exclaim: who is this who shines like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, and majestic as an army? D&C 5:14, 105:31, and 109:73 apply this language to the latter-day Church.

f.w: fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners

chapters.n: Someone — probably the bride — went down to the walnut grove to see if the valley’s vines and pomegranates had begun to bloom.

f.g: A walnut orchard.

chapters.n: Before she knew it, her desire carried her away as if in a royal chariot. The Hebrew is very difficult, and translations vary widely.

f.g: Possibly “my noble people”; the meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: Others call her back: “Come back, Shulamite, so we can see you.” She asks why they would gaze at her as at a festive dance.

f.g: Possibly “woman of Shulem/Shunem,” or a feminine form of Solomon’s name — “the Solomon-ess.”
Or “the dance of Mahanaim” — a joyful dance.

chapters.n: The groom praises his bride from her feet upward, calling her a prince’s daughter — noble in bearing. Her graceful form is like jewelry crafted by a master artist.

f.g: A noble woman — a title of honor, not necessarily literal royalty.
Skilled craftsman.

chapters.n: In the bold imagery of ancient love poetry, he compares her body to a full goblet and a heap of wheat bordered with lilies — signs of abundance and fruitfulness.

f.g: Never lacks mixed wine.
A sign of plenty at harvest.

chapters.n: He repeats an earlier image of gentle twin gazelles.
Her neck is graceful like an ivory tower, her eyes deep and clear like the pools of Heshbon, and her profile noble like a watchtower facing Damascus.

f.g: A city east of the Jordan, known for its reservoirs.
“Daughter of many” — probably a gate of Heshbon.

chapters.n: Her head is majestic like Mount Carmel, and her hair shines with a royal sheen. The king is captivated by her tresses.

f.g: A beautiful, wooded mountain on Israel’s coast.
Better “tresses” — the king is held captive by her locks.

chapters.n: He exclaims how beautiful and delightful she is, his love.
She is tall and graceful like a palm tree, a symbol of beauty and uprightness.

f.g: Tamar in Hebrew, also used as a woman’s name.

chapters.n: He longs to draw close to her, delighting in her fragrance and beauty.
Her kisses are like the finest wine, flowing smoothly. The bride finishes his sentence, saying the wine is “for my beloved.”

f.g: Her kisses or words.

chapters.n: The bride affirms that she belongs to her beloved and that his desire is for her. This reverses the sad note of Genesis 3:16, showing love restored to harmony.

f.r: Genesis 3:16; Song of Solomon 2:16; Song of Solomon 6:3

chapters.n: She invites him to go out with her into the countryside and spend the night in the villages.

f.g: Or “among the henna bushes.”

chapters.n: Let’s rise early, she says, to see whether the vines and pomegranates are blooming. There she will give him her love.

f.g: Grape blossom.

chapters.n: The mandrakes give off their scent, and she has saved every kind of delicious fruit, new and old, for him.

f.g: A plant thought in ancient times to promote love and fertility (Genesis 30:14-16).

chapters.n: The bride wishes she could show affection to her beloved in public as freely as a sister could to a brother, without anyone frowning at her.

f.g: Looked down on or criticized.

chapters.n: She would bring him home to her mother’s house — where she was taught — and share spiced wine with him.
She longs for his tender embrace, repeating an earlier line.
The refrain one last time: do not awaken love before its time. The book teaches patience and purity in love.

f.r: Song of Solomon 2:7; Song of Solomon 3:5

chapters.n: Onlookers see the couple coming from the wilderness, the bride leaning on her husband. She recalls where their love began, under the apple tree near the place he was born.

f.g: A picture of trust and dependence in marriage.

chapters.n: The book’s climax: she asks to be pressed on his heart and arm like a seal — a sign of belonging. True love is as strong as death, and its devotion burns like a fierce flame.

f.g: A signet stamp worn on a cord or ring, marking ownership and identity.
Here, passionate devotion or zeal.
Possibly “the flame of the LORD” (Hebrew shalhebetyah) — the only hint of God’s name in the book.

chapters.n: No flood can put out true love, and no amount of wealth can buy it. Anyone who tried would be scorned. Love is a gift, not a purchase.

f.g: Scorned, despised.

chapters.n: Her brothers speak about their young sister who is not yet grown: how should they protect her until someone asks to marry her?

f.g: Asked for in marriage.

chapters.n: If she is a “wall” — chaste and firm — they will honor her with silver. If she is a “door” — too open — they will protect her with cedar boards.

f.g: A symbol of virtue that resists advances.
A symbol of openness that needs guarding.

chapters.n: The bride declares that she was a “wall” — she kept herself pure — and so she found peace and favor in her husband’s eyes.

f.g: Literally “found peace” (shalom), perhaps a play on Solomon’s name.

chapters.n: Solomon owned a huge vineyard that he rented out to tenants, each paying a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.

f.g: A place name meaning “lord of a multitude”; its location is unknown.
Leased or rented.

chapters.n: But the bride’s own “vineyard” — herself — is hers to give. Solomon can keep his thousand pieces; her love is not for sale.
The groom asks to hear her voice, for his friends are listening and he longs to hear her speak.

f.g: The bride, at home in the gardens of love.

chapters.n: The bride’s final words: come quickly, my beloved, like a gazelle on spice-covered hills. The song ends with love still longing and alive.
